# Accessibility to opportunities {#sec-m4-acessibilidade}

Accessibility is the ease of reaching destinations of interest (jobs, health, education)
from a place, taking into account the actual travel time over the transport network. It is an
indicator that combines, in one number per place, the **distribution of opportunities** and the
**performance of the transport system**. It is the measure that answers the question "whose life
does this project improve?".

The conceptual introduction of this chapter follows Ipea's book *Introduction to urban accessibility*
(Pereira and Herszenhut, 2023), freely available in English at
<https://ipeagit.github.io/intro_access_book/>. It is worth reading in full, especially
chapters 2 (measures) and 3 (calculation in R).

```{r}
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(accessibility)
```

## The two ingredients: where people live, where the opportunities are

The chapter's example is Fortaleza, with data from Ipea's Access to Opportunities project: the
city divided into hexagons of about 0.1 km², with population, income and opportunities in each
one.

```{r}
arquivo <- "dados/brutos/aop_fortaleza.rds"

if (!file.exists(arquivo)) {
  aop <- aopdata::read_access(
    city = "Fortaleza",
    mode = "public_transport",
    year = 2019,
    peak = TRUE,
    geometry = TRUE,
    showProgress = FALSE
  )
  saveRDS(aop, arquivo)
}

aop <- readRDS(arquivo)
```

Before any measure, the two maps every accessibility analysis combines:

```{r}
#| label: fig-ingredientes
#| fig-cap: "Resident population (left) and formal jobs (right) per hexagon, Fortaleza"
#| fig-height: 4.2
mapa_hex <- function(dados, coluna, titulo, paleta) {
  ggplot(dados) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data[[coluna]]), colour = NA) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = paleta, direction = -1, transform = "sqrt",
                         breaks = scales::breaks_pretty(n = 3),
                         labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ","), name = NULL) +
    labs(title = titulo) +
    theme_void(base_size = 9) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.width = unit(1.6, "cm"))
}

patchwork::wrap_plots(
  mapa_hex(aop, "P001", "Where people live", "mako"),
  mapa_hex(aop, "T001", "Where the jobs are", "rocket"),
  nrow = 1
)
```

The mismatch is visible: the population is spread across the whole city, while jobs are concentrated
in the centre and in a few corridors. **Accessibility is the measure of this mismatch, mediated
by the transport system**: how much of the map on the right someone can reach from
each point of the map on the left, within a reasonable time.

## The same yardstick in two places

The most direct way to see this is to choose two starting points and ask: **how many
jobs are within 30 minutes of here?**

For this example, the travel time is **approximate**: straight-line distance divided by
a door-to-door speed of 18 km/h, typical of urban public transport. It is a
simplification, and the section on the `accessibility` package, further down, comes back to it. But it is enough
to show the idea.

```{r}
centros_hex <- sf::st_point_on_surface(sf::st_transform(aop, 31984))   # UTM 24S

# two starting points: the hexagon with the most jobs (the centre) and, among the 10% most
# populous, the farthest from it (a populous neighbourhood on the outskirts)
i_centro <- which.max(aop$T001)
dist_ao_centro <- as.numeric(sf::st_distance(centros_hex, centros_hex[i_centro, ]))
populosos <- which(aop$P001 >= quantile(aop$P001[aop$P001 > 0], 0.9))
i_periferia <- populosos[which.max(dist_ao_centro[populosos])]

tempo_a_partir_de <- function(i, velocidade_kmh = 18) {
  dist_km <- as.numeric(sf::st_distance(centros_hex, centros_hex[i, ])) / 1000
  dist_km / velocidade_kmh * 60
}

origens <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  aop |> dplyr::mutate(origem = "Centre", tempo_min = tempo_a_partir_de(i_centro)),
  aop |> dplyr::mutate(origem = "Outskirts", tempo_min = tempo_a_partir_de(i_periferia))
)

empregos_30 <- origens |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::summarise(empregos = sum(T001[tempo_min <= 30]), .by = origem)
empregos_30
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-regua
#| fig-cap: "Approximate travel time from two points in Fortaleza. The highlighted hexagons are within 30 minutes."
#| fig-height: 4.4
rotulos <- setNames(
  paste0(empregos_30$origem, ": ",
         scales::label_number(big.mark = ",")(empregos_30$empregos),
         " jobs within 30 min"),
  empregos_30$origem
)

pontos_partida <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  aop[i_centro, ] |> dplyr::mutate(origem = "Centre"),
  aop[i_periferia, ] |> dplyr::mutate(origem = "Outskirts")
) |>
  sf::st_point_on_surface()

ggplot(origens) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cut(tempo_min, c(0, 15, 30, 45, 60, Inf),
                         labels = c("up to 15", "15 to 30", "30 to 45", "45 to 60", "over 60"),
                         include.lowest = TRUE)),
          colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = pontos_partida, shape = 21, size = 3, fill = "white", stroke = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~origem, labeller = labeller(origem = rotulos)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#1a5b8a", "#5b9bc8", "#e8e8e8", "#f2f2f2", "#fafafa"),
                    name = "minutes") +
  theme_void(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The yardstick is the same, 30 minutes; the result is not. Someone living in the centre reaches something like three
times more jobs than someone living in the outlying neighbourhood. And in practice the difference is even
bigger, because public transport on the outskirts is usually slower and less frequent
than the 18 km/h assumed here. Doing this sum for **every** hexagon is computing an
accessibility measure.

## Place-based and person-based measures

Ipea's book organises the measures into two broad groups:

- **Place-based**: they assign a level of access to each place (hexagon, tract, zone), and
  everyone who lives there gets the same value. They reflect the distribution of
  opportunities and the network's performance, but not the characteristics of each person. They need
  little data, are easy to compute and to communicate. They are the ones used in planning, and the
  ones in this chapter.
- **Person-based**: they consider age, income, disability, the day's activity schedule.
  They are more realistic, but they require travel diaries or an origin–destination survey, are heavy to
  compute and hard to sum up in one indicator.

## Place-based measures

| Measure | Question it answers | In words | Function |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Minimum time | how long to the nearest hospital? | the shortest time to the nearest opportunity | `cost_to_closest()` |
| Cumulative opportunities | how many jobs can I reach within 30 minutes? | sum of the opportunities within the time limit | `cumulative_cutoff()` |
| Gravity | how many opportunities, discounting the farthest? | sum of the opportunities, each with a weight that falls with time | `gravity()` |
| Competition (2SFCA, BFCA) | how many opportunities per person, given the competition? | like gravity, dividing each opportunity by everyone who can also reach it | `floating_catchment_area()` |

The previous figure was a **cumulative** measure for two points. The difference between the measures
lies in the **weight** each gives an opportunity according to the time to reach it:

```{r}
#| label: fig-decaimento
#| fig-cap: "Decay functions: the weight given to an opportunity according to travel time"
#| fig-height: 3.4
t <- 0:90
data.frame(
  minutos = rep(t, 3),
  peso = c(exp(-0.05 * t),
           as.numeric(t <= 30),
           pmax(0, 1 - t / 60)),
  funcao = rep(c("exponential (0.05)", "cumulative (30 min)", "linear (60 min)"),
               each = length(t))
) |>
  ggplot(aes(minutos, peso, colour = funcao)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#1a5b8a", "#b3402a", "#e0a03f"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Travel time (min)", y = "Weight of the opportunity") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

- The **cumulative** one is the red step: weight 1 up to 30 minutes, zero afterwards. It is the most used
  because it is the easiest to communicate ("jobs accessible within 30 minutes"). The cost is treating a
  job 29 minutes away as fully accessible and one 31 minutes away as inaccessible, and a job 5
  minutes away the same as one 29 minutes away.
- The **gravity** measure smooths the step: the exponential gives a lot of weight to what is near and little
  to what is far. It is the most technically defensible, but the decay parameter needs to
  be calibrated with travel data, and the final number is hard to explain in a meeting.
- The **minimum time** adds nothing up: it only looks at the nearest opportunity. It is the most suitable
  for essential and rare services (a high-complexity hospital), but it ignores how many
  opportunities exist and whether the nearest one is overloaded.
- The **competition** measures take into account that an ICU bed or a school place is contested
  by everyone who can reach it. They are the most complete for services with limited capacity, and the
  hardest to interpret.

The choice changes the result, and that is why it must be stated in the report.

## Ready-made data: `aopdata`

Ipea's Access to Opportunities project publishes, for 20 Brazilian cities, the indicators
already computed on a hexagonal grid, with population, income, race and opportunities per hexagon. It is the
`aop` object we loaded at the start. For a diagnosis, it is the quickest route.

```{r}
dim(aop)
names(aop) |> head(30)
```

The column names follow a documented pattern: `P001` is the total population, `R001` the per capita
income, `T001` the total number of jobs, and the access indicators combine the type of measure
(`CMA` = active cumulative, `TMI` = minimum time), the activity (`TT` = all jobs,
`ST` = health, `ET` = education) and the time limit.

```{r}
cols_cma <- grep("^CMATT", names(aop), value = TRUE)
cols_cma

# income stratum column: the package has quintile and decile (R002 and R003).
# Check in the dictionary which is which before labelling the chart:
# aopdata::aopdata_dictionary(lang = "en")
col_renda <- dplyr::intersect(c("R002", "R003"), names(aop))[1]
col_renda
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-aop-mapa
#| fig-cap: "Jobs accessible within 60 minutes by public transport in Fortaleza"
#| fig-height: 5
col_60 <- dplyr::intersect(c("CMATT60"), names(aop))[1]

if (!is.na(col_60)) {
  aop_plot <- aop |>
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(.data[[col_60]]), P001 > 0) |>
    dplyr::mutate(acesso = .data[[col_60]])

  ggplot(aop_plot) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = acesso), colour = NA) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "inferno", direction = -1,
                         labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ","),
                         name = "Jobs\nwithin 60 min") +
    labs(caption = "Source: Ipea, Access to Opportunities Project (aopdata), 2019.") +
    theme_void(base_size = 9)
}
```

### Accessibility and inequality

The indicator gains meaning when combined with who lives in each place:

```{r}
if (!is.na(col_60)) {
  aop |>
    sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
    dplyr::filter(P001 > 0, !is.na(.data[[col_60]]), !is.na(.data[[col_renda]])) |>
    dplyr::mutate(estrato_renda = .data[[col_renda]]) |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      pessoas = sum(P001),
      # as.numeric(): P001 and access are integers, and the product overflows the integer limit
      acesso_medio = round(weighted.mean(as.numeric(.data[[col_60]]), P001, na.rm = TRUE)),
      .by = estrato_renda
    ) |>
    dplyr::arrange(estrato_renda) |>
    dplyr::rename(`Income stratum` = estrato_renda, `Population` = pessoas,
           `Jobs accessible within 60 min (mean)` = acesso_medio) |>
    knitr::kable(align = "lrr")
}
```

The typical reading of this kind of table (the poorest strata with less access) is the
main equity argument in the appraisal of urban transport projects. The columns
`R002` and `R003` hold the income strata (quintile and decile); check in the package's dictionary
which is which before labelling the chart, because swapping them reverses the reading.

## Computing from scratch: the `accessibility` package

When the city is not in `aopdata`, or when you want to assess a **scenario** (a new
route, a route removed), you have to compute it. The input is a travel time matrix,
usually coming from `r5r` (@sec-m4-r5r), and a land use table.

To demonstrate the functions in a runnable way, we will build an **approximate** time matrix
from the distances between the hexagons, assuming an average speed.

```{r}
set.seed(2026)

hex <- aop |>
  dplyr::filter(P001 > 0) |>
  dplyr::select(id_hex, P001, T001, dplyr::all_of(col_renda)) |>
  dplyr::slice_sample(n = 250)          # a sample, so that the example runs quickly

centros <- sf::st_point_on_surface(sf::st_transform(hex, 31984))   # UTM 24S (Fortaleza)

d <- sf::st_distance(centros) |> units::set_units(km) |> as.numeric()
d <- matrix(d, nrow = nrow(hex))

velocidade_kmh <- 18    # typical door-to-door speed of urban public transport

matriz <- expand.grid(from_id = hex$id_hex, to_id = hex$id_hex,
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::mutate(travel_time = round(as.vector(d) / velocidade_kmh * 60, 1)) |>
  dplyr::filter(travel_time <= 90)

uso_solo <- hex |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::rename(id = id_hex, populacao = P001, empregos = T001)

head(matriz, 3)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
This matrix is **illustrative**: straight-line distance divided by an average speed is not
public transport travel time. It serves to show how the `accessibility` functions
work. In any real use, the matrix comes from `r5r`, with the network, the GTFS and the
departure time. The difference between the two is large, especially in cities with physical
barriers.
:::

```{r}
# 1. cumulative opportunities within 30, 60 and 90 minutes
cma <- accessibility::cumulative_cutoff(
  travel_matrix = matriz,
  land_use_data = uso_solo,
  opportunity   = "empregos",
  travel_cost   = "travel_time",
  cutoff        = c(30, 60, 90)
)

head(cma, 4)
```

```{r}
# 2. time to the nearest opportunity
tmi <- accessibility::cost_to_closest(
  travel_matrix = matriz,
  land_use_data = uso_solo,
  opportunity   = "empregos",
  travel_cost   = "travel_time",
  n             = 1
)

summary(tmi[[ncol(tmi)]])   # the last column holds the time to the nearest opportunity
```

```{r}
# 3. gravity measure, with exponential decay
grav <- accessibility::gravity(
  travel_matrix = matriz,
  land_use_data = uso_solo,
  opportunity   = "empregos",
  travel_cost   = "travel_time",
  decay_function = accessibility::decay_exponential(decay_value = 0.05)
)

head(grav, 4)
```

## Comparing scenarios

The most valuable application in planning is not the absolute value of the indicator. It is the
**difference between two scenarios**. So that the example runs, the scenario is also illustrative: a
new, hypothetical route that cuts by 40% the time of trips starting or ending in the western
half of the sample. With the real network, the two matrices come from `r5r`: the current one and the one computed with the
edited GTFS, as in @sec-m4-r5r.

The limit is **30 minutes**, not 60, for a reason that applies to any study: with 60
minutes, almost every hexagon in the sample already reaches almost every job, and no
intervention shows up in the indicator. A cumulative measure only shows a difference when the time
limit is below the point at which it saturates.

```{r}
# illustrative scenario: the new route serves the hexagons in the western half of the sample
x <- sf::st_coordinates(centros)[, "X"]
oeste <- hex$id_hex[x < stats::median(x)]

matriz_atual   <- matriz
matriz_cenario <- matriz |>
  dplyr::mutate(travel_time = dplyr::if_else(from_id %in% oeste | to_id %in% oeste,
                                             travel_time * 0.60, travel_time))

acesso_atual  <- accessibility::cumulative_cutoff(matriz_atual,  uso_solo, "empregos", "travel_time", 30)
acesso_novo   <- accessibility::cumulative_cutoff(matriz_cenario, uso_solo, "empregos", "travel_time", 30)

comparacao <- acesso_atual |>
  dplyr::rename(acesso_atual = empregos) |>
  dplyr::left_join(dplyr::rename(acesso_novo, acesso_novo = empregos), by = "id") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    variacao_abs = acesso_novo - acesso_atual,
    # with no access in the current scenario, the percentage change does not exist
    variacao_pct = dplyr::if_else(acesso_atual > 0, 100 * (acesso_novo / acesso_atual - 1), NA_real_)
  ) |>
  dplyr::left_join(uso_solo, by = "id")

# the number that matters to the manager: how many people gained access, and who they are
comparacao |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    pessoas_beneficiadas = sum(populacao[variacao_abs > 0]),
    ganho_medio_pct = weighted.mean(variacao_pct, populacao, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = dplyr::all_of(col_renda)
  )
```

It is this table, people benefiting by income bracket, that turns a transport analysis
into a public policy argument. The final project
(@sec-m5-projeto) follows exactly this path.
